job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Rosa Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Rosa, and thank you for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the first year of a master's in machine learning at Tessing University, living in a student house with four people and one bathroom. My day starts at the library at eight, where I write code with an AI assistant open next to me, and then I have a seminar on model evaluation. My bachelor's was software engineering, and I did two internships, one at a logistics startup and one at a hospital data team. In the evenings I run a small reading group about AI and labour. What wears me out is how fast the tools change under my feet, though honestly I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised and I'd even be a bit relieved. At work I'd say let's use the tools that actually save time and stop pretending they're magic. To friends I'd say good, now we can have a sensible conversation about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my plans don't need to be so urgent. I'd still do my master's, still work in machine learning, but I'd care more about evaluating tools than building shiny things. And honestly I'd worry about the people who invested their careers in the hype and then get dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and take a job on a team that tests and audits models, like the hospital data team I interned with. I'd keep using AI tools daily because they're quick, and I'd write up my reading group's notes as a blog. And I'd put a little money into a union-run savings scheme my cousin told me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's a slower world but a steady one, and there are lots of jobs where I'd be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. If it's mostly hype, doesn't that undercut your own field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Some roles in my field wouldn't exist. But a plateau still leaves plenty of jobs around data and evaluation, and I've got the skills. It would just be a less glamorous career than I imagined as a teenager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you if nothing big changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, honestly. My student house is cheap, but a flat near the hospital would cost half a graduate salary. And my mum is a nurse on a ward that's short of staff, and I worry about her, since AI doesn't fix that either.

To friends I'd say a plateau lets us have a **sensible conversation**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here and it's uneven, and we should name who is being hit. At work I'd propose that every team writes down which tasks it moves to software and what happens to the people who did them. Online I'd share data on junior hiring, because that's where the first signs show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my role is in the blast zone. Coding, checking and writing are the tasks the card says move first, and I do them all, so the entry-level coding job I trained for may be half what it was. But I also know how to use these tools well, so I'd be at the right end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to roles that combine model evaluation with domain knowledge, like health data, where you need a human to be accountable. I'd start a small portfolio project for a hospital group, probably with my intern contact there. And I'd get more active in my labour reading group and push for a graduate rights statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it also gives me energy. I'm in the middle of the change instead of watching it from outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My housemate Kofi, who's doing a plain software degree without any AI side. He writes solid code but the junior job market is shrinking beneath him. I've offered to pair with him, but I worry I'm only making myself feel better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why accountability? What do you mean by a human being accountable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a model wrongly flags a patient, someone has to answer for it, and that someone needs to understand the model well enough to be trusted. That's a job that grows when AI does more. I'd like to be the person in the room who can say what the model got wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and I'd say it loudly, with figures. I'd tell my reading group and our student union that we need emergency measures: income support, retraining funds and a pause on firing juniors. And I'd tell friends that 2028 is about as long as it takes to finish a master's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think everything I'm studying becomes cheap, fast, and I'm the one who can't explain why it still matters. If almost any thinking work is done better and cheaper by 2028, the job I'm training for isn't there. I have money and no debt, so I'm not starving, but I'm shaken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to get into any role where I stay close to the systems, like an audit, safety or policy job, even a junior one. I'd learn the best tools hard and quickly. And I'd talk to my mum about a plan, since the nurse side of the family might do well in a robot-delayed world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm moving fast, not freezing, but I can't pretend it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you more anxious for yourself or for others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For others, mostly, which maybe is a way of avoiding myself. My cushion lets me think big. For friends without a family to back them, it's a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month after the announcement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call a meeting of the reading group and turn it into something practical, like a skills swap and a hardship fund. I'd write to my MP with real numbers. And I'd apply to five safety and audit teams the same week, because action beats scrolling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build real protections if we start now. I'd push my university to add courses on evaluation and policy. And I'd tell friends it's a good moment to find where humans stay accountable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay but stretched. I'd be 29 in 2031, probably a few years into audit or safety work, which is where I'd want to be. The danger is that thinking AI reaches my job before I've built a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, join an audit or safety team, and write publicly about what I'm learning. I'd take a part-time policy fellowship if I could. And I'd save a third of my salary, since I might retrain after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. Five years is a real runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the five-year picture differ from the two-year one for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get to choose instead of reacting. With two years I'd take whatever job keeps me near the systems, but with five I can aim for a particular team and build a track record. It lowers the fear and raises the stakes of being good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it came a year early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on the savings, and I'd go to the policy people and say I'm ready to work. I'd be annoyed with myself for not building more, but I'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should be careful not to waste it. I'd tell friends to learn to evaluate AI, not just use it. And I'd tell my reading group it's time to write down the rules we'd actually want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good. I'd be 34 by 2036, with maybe ten years in audit and safety, and I'd have time to move up. I'd worry about the wider world more than about my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, build my career on a safety team, and keep a part-time research habit. I'd keep trying every new tool, because that's how I learn. I'd also help set up a university course for others who want to move into this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a little excited. A decade lets me do it carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bothers you most in the long version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the gains won't be shared. If ten years pass and a few companies own everything, my decade of calm career-building won't help anyone else. I'd want to spend part of it on policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what do you actually do about that, besides worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join a union for tech workers, give a regular chunk of my salary to the groups working on this, and vote in every election. It sounds small, but I'd rather do small things for ten years than nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one, by a lot. A few years is enough for me to cope, but not enough for most people I know to retrain, find new work and sort out their families. What would help is support that arrives early: income help, honest guidance from universities and firms that keep hiring juniors. I'd want organised groups, like unions, to have a voice at the table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what I'd give up to slow it down. I'd honestly accept a slower, less exciting version if it meant everyone had more time. My friends think that's a strange thing for someone studying AI to say.

headlineQuote: I'd honestly accept a slower, less exciting version if it meant everyone had more time.
portrait: Rosa is 24, doing a **master's** in machine learning at Tessing University and living in a shared student house.
She is curious, uses **AI tools daily**, and leans left, favouring unions, regulation and public support.
Her cushion is strong, so her worry is mostly for **others** with less family backing.
She turns anxiety into action quickly with reading groups, letters and applications.
She aims for audit and safety work where a human must be **accountable**.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because most people she knows can't retrain in time.
whatWouldHelp: **Early support** such as income help, honest guidance and firms that keep hiring juniors.
Unions and organised groups having a **voice** at the table.
